patient.name: Desmond Hayes
patient.complaint: Sudden severe abdominal pain going through to his back, then collapse at home
background: AAA found at NHS screening aged 65 (3.4 cm); last scan 5.2 cm, then missed two appointments
Smoked 40 a day for 50 years; severe COPD
Lives with his wife in Croydon

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with an older male smoker, sudden abdominal or back pain, hypotension and a pulsatile mass (ruptured AAA), or an asymptomatic pulsatile mass found on examination.

points: Desmond, 74, felt a **sudden tearing pain** in his abdomen and **back**.
He **collapsed** in the kitchen; his wife called 999.

steps.lead: Sudden abdominal/back pain with **hypotension** and **tachycardia** in a man with a known AAA: this is **rupture** until proven otherwise.

visual.title: Where Desmond's pain is
visual.caption: Central abdominal pain that goes through to the **back** or **left flank**.

points: Abdomen tender; peripheries cold and mottled.

steps.lead: Desmond's **pulsatile abdominal mass** is the classic AAA sign; a thoracic aneurysm would instead cause chest pain and compression symptoms.
Desmond's aorta, normally about 2 cm, has grown past **5 cm**: well over **1.5 times** normal, and infrarenal.
Fifty years of **smoking**, plus hypertension and atherosclerosis: Desmond carries the AAA risk profile.

steps.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
steps.r: Known AAA, sudden abdominal/back pain, shock and a pulsatile mass = **ruptured AAA**. Dissection gives tearing chest pain radiating to the back.

steps.title: Abdominal pain to the back: spot the difference
head: Ruptured AAA
Renal colic
Pancreatitis
Dissection

steps.text: An older man with first-ever **'renal colic'** and low BP is a **ruptured AAA** until proven otherwise. Do not be reassured by microscopic haematuria.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?' (abdominal ultrasound), questions on screening (men in the year they turn 65) and CT angiography for planning repair.

points: Resus: two large-bore cannulas, bloods, **crossmatch** sent.
Bedside ultrasound by the ED consultant.

steps.lead: Desmond was found through **screening** in the year he turned **65**. His bedside **ultrasound** now measures the aorta at 6.3 cm.

visual.title: Aortic diameter on ultrasound
visual.label: Desmond 6.3 cm
visual.caption: Size decides everything: surveillance below 5.5 cm, **repair** at 5.5 cm or more.

steps.lead: **Ultrasound** found and followed Desmond's aneurysm; **CT** is what the surgeons use to plan the repair.

steps.title: Desmond's resus bloods
steps.text: Falling Hb and rising lactate: he is **bleeding** and underperfused.

steps.q: Desmond's BP responds to a small fluid bolus and holds at 92 systolic. What is the role of CT now?
o: CT angiogram to plan the repair, without delaying theatre
CT is never used in AAA
Ultrasound alone is enough to plan surgery
steps.r: **CT angiogram** shows the leak and whether the anatomy suits **EVAR**. A patient who stays unstable goes straight to theatre.

steps.lead: Desmond's **CT angiogram** confirms a retroperitoneal rupture and anatomy that is **suitable for EVAR**.

steps.title: AAA investigation
nodes: Men in the year they turn 65: screening ultrasound
Suspected AAA: abdominal ultrasound, measure diameter
Suspected rupture: crossmatch, imaging only if stable

steps.text: Screening is **one** ultrasound for men in the year they turn **65**. Men over 65 who were never screened can ask for one.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate management?' by size: <3 cm discharge, 3–4.4 cm yearly scan, 4.5–5.4 cm 3-monthly, ≥5.5 cm (or symptomatic or growing >1 cm/year) surgery within 2 weeks. Rupture: crossmatch 6 units and emergency surgery.

steps.lead: Desmond's team **crossmatch 6 units** and take him for **emergency surgery** within the hour.

steps.q: What is the priority for Desmond now?
o: Admit to the ward and repeat ultrasound tomorrow
steps.r: Ruptured AAA: **crossmatch (commonly 6 units)** and **emergency surgery**. Any delay is fatal.

steps.title: Ruptured AAA: the first hour
nodes: Cautious fluids: keep him conscious, not normotensive

steps.lead: Open repair is usually first-line, but Desmond's **severe COPD** is a **major anaesthetic risk**, so he has **EVAR** instead.

steps.q: Why is EVAR chosen for Desmond rather than open repair?
o: Severe COPD makes major anaesthesia and laparotomy high risk
steps.r: **EVAR** avoids a laparotomy, so it suits patients **unfit for open repair**. It needs lifelong imaging for endoleak.

visual.title: Desmond's aortic diameter over the years
visual.caption: Small at 65 (yearly scans), medium from 70 (3-monthly). Reaching **5.5 cm** should have triggered referral for repair.

steps.lead: Desmond's surveillance followed the size bands; **missed scans** meant nobody saw him pass 5.5 cm. Smoking cessation and **BP control** were key.
Desmond's pathway follows the **NHS AAA screening programme** and **NICE** AAA guidance.

steps.text: Do not swap the intervals: **small (3–4.4 cm) = yearly**, **medium (4.5–5.4 cm) = every 3 months**. Below 3 cm needs no further scans.
Urgent referral **within 2 weeks** if symptomatic, **≥5.5 cm**, or growing **>1 cm/year**. Any aneurysm >3 cm is referred to vascular surgeons within 12 weeks.

science.exam: Science questions ask about the wall weakness (elastin and collagen breakdown), why rupture risk climbs steeply with size (Laplace's law) or why EVAR needs long-term follow-up (endoleak).

steps.title: How Desmond's aneurysm grew
nodes: Elastin and collagen in the media degraded

steps.lead: Desmond's smoking drove the **inflammation** and **MMP** activity that broke down his aortic wall; his hypertension added wall stress.
As Desmond's aorta widened, **wall tension** rose with it, so his rupture risk climbed **disproportionately** as he grew past 5.5 cm.

steps.q: By Laplace's law, if pressure stays the same and the radius doubles, wall tension:
steps.r: Laplace: tension ∝ **pressure × radius**. Bigger aneurysm = more tension = more dilation, a vicious cycle.

steps.lead: Desmond's EVAR avoids a laparotomy, lowering his **perioperative** risk, but he will need lifelong scans for **endoleak**.

steps.title: EVAR vs open repair
head: EVAR
Open repair
rows: Unfit for open repair, hostile abdomen

steps.text: An **endoleak** is blood still flowing into the aneurysm sac outside the stent graft; the sac stays pressurised and can still grow or rupture.

o: Dilation to at least 1.5 times normal diameter
mcq.r: Permanent dilation to **≥1.5x** normal diameter. An intimal tear is dissection.

glossary.Aneurysm: Permanent dilation of an artery to at least 1.5 times its normal diameter.
glossary.AAA: Abdominal aortic aneurysm, usually below the renal arteries.
glossary.Infrarenal: Below the level of the renal arteries; where most AAAs arise.
glossary.Thoracic aortic aneurysm: An aneurysm of the aorta in the chest, causing chest pain and compression symptoms.
glossary.Pulsatile mass: A swelling that throbs with each heartbeat.
glossary.Expansile: Pushes the examiner's fingers apart, not just up, suggesting an aneurysm rather than a transmitted pulse.
glossary.Rupture: Bursting of the aneurysm wall, causing massive internal bleeding.
glossary.Retroperitoneal: Behind the peritoneum; most AAA ruptures bleed here at first.
glossary.EVAR: Endovascular aneurysm repair: a stent graft placed through the femoral arteries, avoiding a laparotomy.
glossary.Open aortic repair: Replacing the aneurysmal aorta with a synthetic graft through a laparotomy.
glossary.Endoleak: Persistent blood flow into the aneurysm sac outside an EVAR stent graft.
glossary.Laparotomy: Open abdominal surgery through a large incision.
glossary.Hostile abdomen: An abdomen with dense adhesions or previous surgery that makes open repair risky.
glossary.Horseshoe kidney: Congenitally fused kidneys lying across the aorta, which complicates open repair.
glossary.Stoma: An opening of bowel onto the abdominal wall, making open repair harder.
glossary.Crossmatch: Testing donor blood against the patient's blood so units are ready for transfusion.
glossary.CT angiogram: CT scan with IV contrast showing the aorta's size, shape and leaks; used to plan EVAR.
glossary.NHS AAA screening programme: A one-off abdominal ultrasound offered to men in the year they turn 65.
glossary.Surveillance: Repeat ultrasound scans at set intervals to watch an aneurysm's growth.
glossary.Laplace's law: Wall tension is proportional to pressure times radius, so wider aneurysms are under more tension.
glossary.Matrix metalloproteinases: Enzymes that break down elastin and collagen in the aortic wall.
glossary.Elastin: A stretchy protein in the aortic media that lets it recoil.
glossary.Collagen: A strong structural protein in the aortic wall that resists rupture.
glossary.Media: The middle, muscular and elastic layer of the artery wall.
glossary.Aortic dissection: A tear in the aortic intima letting blood split the wall, causing tearing chest pain.
glossary.Renal colic: Severe loin-to-groin pain from a kidney stone; a classic misdiagnosis for ruptured AAA.
glossary.Permissive hypotension: Accepting a lower blood pressure in bleeding patients to avoid worsening the haemorrhage.
glossary.COPD: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, which raises anaesthetic risk.
glossary.Major haemorrhage protocol: A hospital system to deliver large amounts of blood products quickly.
glossary.Haemodynamic instability: Low blood pressure and fast pulse showing poor circulation.

technique.stem: A 71 year old man has a 1 hour history of severe left loin pain radiating to his groin. He has never had kidney stones. He smokes 30 cigarettes a day. His pulse rate is 122 bpm and BP 88/56 mmHg. He is pale and sweaty. Urinalysis shows a trace of blood.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question: is this really renal colic?
An older male smoker with first-ever 'renal colic' and **shock**: ruptured AAA mimics colic.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Pyelonephritis gives fever and dysuria, not sudden shock.
Diverticulitis gives LIF pain and fever.
Renal colic does not cause hypotension; trace blood is common in AAA rupture too.
Torsion affects young males with testicular pain.

steps.x: **D.** Rule: older man + first 'renal colic' + low BP = ruptured AAA.

technique.stem: A 76 year old man has sudden severe abdominal and back pain. He has a known 5.4 cm abdominal aortic aneurysm. His pulse rate is 130 bpm and BP 78/44 mmHg. A vascular surgeon is on the way.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate immediate investigation?

steps.x: Immediate investigation in an unstable suspected rupture.

clues: sudden severe abdominal and back pain
steps.x: Known AAA + pain + shock = **rupture**; he is too unstable for CT.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Get blood ready: **crossmatch (commonly 6 units)**, then theatre.

elim: AXR adds nothing and wastes time.
CT is for stable patients; this man is shocked.
Erect CXR looks for perforation.
Amylase helps in pancreatitis, not here.

steps.x: **B.** Rule: unstable ruptured AAA = crossmatch and theatre, no CT.

technique.stem: A 70 year old man has a 6.0 cm abdominal aortic aneurysm on ultrasound. He has severe heart failure and has had several previous laparotomies for Crohn's disease, with an ileostomy. A CT angiogram shows anatomy suitable for an endovascular graft.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate management?

steps.x: A repair question: is he fit for open surgery?

clues: anatomy suitable for an endovascular graft
steps.x: ≥5.5 cm needs repair. Major anaesthetic risk, hostile abdomen and a stoma make open repair unsuitable.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Open repair is first-line only if fit; he is not.
Yearly scans are for 3–4.4 cm.
3-monthly scans are for 4.5–5.4 cm.
Risk-factor control alone leaves a 6 cm aneurysm untreated.

steps.x: **A.** Rule: ≥5.5 cm = repair; open first-line, EVAR if unsuitable for open.

technique.stem: A 79 year old man had endovascular aneurysm repair 3 years ago. A follow-up CT shows contrast flowing into the aneurysm sac outside the stent graft, and the sac has enlarged.
technique.q: Which best explains why he needs further intervention?

steps.x: A mechanism question about EVAR follow-up.

clues: contrast flowing into the aneurysm sac outside the stent graft
steps.x: Blood still entering the sac after EVAR.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Endoleak**: the reason EVAR has more long-term re-interventions.

elim: Anastomotic dehiscence is a sutured (open) repair problem.
Infection gives fever and gas around the graft.
Incisional hernia follows laparotomy, not EVAR.
EVAR has only small groin wounds.

steps.x: **B.** Rule: EVAR = lower early mortality, but endoleak means lifelong surveillance.

practice.stem: A 69 year old man collapses at home with sudden severe central abdominal pain radiating to his back. He smokes and has hypertension. His pulse rate is 124 bpm, BP 82/50 mmHg and respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute. A pulsatile, expansile mass is felt above the umbilicus.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Sudden abdominal/back pain, shock and a pulsatile expansile mass in an older male smoker is a ruptured AAA.

steps.x: Diagnosis: abdominal pain to the back with shock.

clues: sudden severe central abdominal pain radiating to his back
steps.x: Smoker, back pain, hypotension, pulsatile mass.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Pancreatitis rarely causes this shock so suddenly and has no pulsatile mass.
Dissection gives tearing chest pain to the back.
Perforation gives a rigid abdomen without a pulsatile mass.
Renal colic does not cause shock.

steps.x: **E.** Pain + shock + pulsatile mass = ruptured AAA.

practice.stem: A 70 year old man who smokes sees his GP for a routine check. He has no symptoms. On abdominal examination there is a non-tender, pulsatile, expansile mass in the epigastrium. His BP is 150/90 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: An asymptomatic pulsatile, expansile epigastric mass in an older male smoker is an AAA. A mass overlying the aorta transmits pulsation but is not expansile.

steps.x: Diagnosis: what is an expansile mass?

clues: pulsatile, expansile mass in the epigastrium
steps.x: Expansile, not just pulsatile: the mass itself is the artery.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Colorectal carcinoma gives bowel symptoms and is not expansile.
Hepatomegaly is in the RUQ and moves with respiration.
Horseshoe kidney is rarely felt and not expansile.
A pseudocyst follows pancreatitis and only transmits pulsation.

practice.stem: A 68 year old man with long-standing hypertension has a 3 month history of dull central chest pain, a hoarse voice and difficulty swallowing. He has not lost weight. His BP is 168/96 mmHg. A chest X-ray shows a widened mediastinum.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Chest pain with compression of surrounding structures (recurrent laryngeal nerve, oesophagus) and a widened mediastinum in a hypertensive man suggests a thoracic aortic aneurysm.

steps.x: Diagnosis: chest pain plus compression symptoms.
Compression of the recurrent laryngeal nerve and oesophagus by a mediastinal mass; no weight loss.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Achalasia causes dysphagia but not hoarseness or a widened mediastinum.
Bronchial carcinoma usually causes weight loss, cough and haemoptysis.
Oesophageal cancer causes progressive dysphagia and weight loss.
A goitre is a neck mass.

steps.x: **D.** Chest pain + compression symptoms = thoracic aneurysm.

practice.stem: A 66 year old man has an abdominal aortic aneurysm found on screening. He asks which of his habits or conditions most contributed to it.
practice.q: Which is the strongest risk factor for his condition?
practice.e: Smoking is the strongest risk factor for AAA. Diabetes is not a risk factor and AAA is more common in men.

clues: abdominal aortic aneurysm found on screening
steps.x: AAA risk factors: smoking, hypertension, atherosclerosis, CKD, family history.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Diabetes is not a recognised AAA risk factor.
AAA is commoner in men.
Hyperlipidaemia contributes via atherosclerosis but is weaker.
Hypertension is a risk factor, but weaker than smoking.

practice.stem: A 65 year old man attends his NHS AAA screening appointment. Ultrasound shows an infrarenal aortic diameter of 5.0 cm. He has no symptoms. His BP is 142/86 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on abdominal examination?
o: Pulsatile expansile mass above the umbilicus
practice.e: A 5 cm AAA is classically felt as a pulsatile, expansile mass above the umbilicus (the aorta divides at about the umbilicus).

steps.x: A finding question: what would you feel?

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: A hepatic bruit suggests hepatocellular carcinoma or alcoholic hepatitis.
Caput medusae is portal hypertension.
Shifting dullness is ascites.
Succussion splash is gastric outlet obstruction.

practice.stem: A 78 year old man with a known 5.9 cm abdominal aortic aneurysm, awaiting surgery, has sudden severe back pain and feels faint. His pulse rate is 132 bpm and BP 80/48 mmHg. He is pale and clammy.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his presentation?
practice.e: A large known AAA with sudden back pain, hypotension and tachycardia means rupture, the major complication.

steps.x: A cause question in a known AAA.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Dissection gives tearing chest pain and pulse deficits.
Mesenteric ischaemia gives abdominal pain out of proportion, often with AF.
Renal colic does not cause shock.
Vertebral collapse causes back pain without shock.

steps.x: **D.** Known AAA + back pain + shock = rupture.

practice.stem: A 65 year old man receives a letter inviting him to the NHS abdominal aortic aneurysm screening programme. He has no symptoms.
practice.q: Which investigation will he be offered?
practice.e: AAA screening is a single abdominal ultrasound measuring aortic diameter, offered to men in the year they turn 65.

steps.x: Men in the year they turn 65 are screened.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: AXR cannot measure the aorta reliably.
CTA is for planning repair.
MRA is not used for screening.
Lipids assess cardiovascular risk, not AAA.

practice.stem: A 72 year old man has a 5.8 cm abdominal aortic aneurysm on ultrasound and has been referred for repair. The vascular surgeon wants to know whether he is suitable for an endovascular graft.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
practice.e: CT angiography is the gold standard for surgical planning and determines suitability for EVAR.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: AXR gives no anatomical detail.
Echo assesses the heart for anaesthesia, not EVAR anatomy.
MRI spine is irrelevant.
Rescanning delays a repair that is already indicated.

practice.stem: A 67 year old man has an abdominal aortic aneurysm of 4.8 cm on ultrasound. He has no symptoms. It measured 4.6 cm a year ago. His BP is 136/82 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Urgent referral for surgery within 2 weeks
practice.e: A medium AAA (4.5–5.4 cm) that is asymptomatic and growing slowly is rescanned every 3 months. Yearly scans are for small (3–4.4 cm) aneurysms.

steps.x: A surveillance question: place the diameter in its band.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Emergency repair is for rupture.
No scanning is only for <3 cm.
Yearly is for 3–4.4 cm.
2-week referral needs ≥5.5 cm, symptoms or >1 cm/year growth.

practice.stem: A 71 year old man has an asymptomatic abdominal aortic aneurysm. It measured 5.0 cm six months ago and now measures 5.6 cm. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 138/84 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Start a statin and review in 6 months
practice.e: Diameter ≥5.5 cm (and growth >1 cm/year) is an indication for urgent referral for surgery within 2 weeks.

steps.x: Now ≥5.5 cm, and growing at 1.2 cm/year.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: A 5.6 cm aneurysm must not be discharged.
3-monthly scans are for 4.5–5.4 cm.
Yearly scans are for 3–4.4 cm.
A statin helps risk but delays needed repair.

steps.x: **E.** ≥5.5 cm or >1 cm/year = surgery within 2 weeks.

practice.stem: A 74 year old man with a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm is in the resuscitation room. Blood has been crossmatched. His pulse rate is 128 bpm and BP 84/50 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
practice.e: A ruptured AAA needs crossmatched blood (commonly 6 units) and emergency surgery. Delay is fatal.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Elective timing is for intact aneurysms.
Observation of a rupture is fatal.
Surveillance is for small intact aneurysms.
Thrombolysis would worsen bleeding.

practice.stem: A 70 year old man's abdominal aortic aneurysm has grown from 4.0 cm to 6.0 cm. His surgeon explains that the risk of rupture has risen far more than the 50% increase in diameter.
practice.e: Laplace's law: wall tension is proportional to pressure times radius, so larger aneurysms carry disproportionately higher wall tension and rupture risk.

steps.x: Bigger radius → more wall tension → more dilation and rupture.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Bernoulli relates flow velocity and pressure.
Fick's law describes diffusion.
Poiseuille's law describes flow resistance.
Starling's law relates to cardiac filling or capillary fluid exchange.
